name: Sparsity against explained behaviour
summary: A scatter in which every dot is one trained sparse autoencoder, placed by how many features fire per token against how much of the MLP's loss contribution its reconstruction recovers. It turns the choice of sparsity penalty and dictionary width into a visible exchange rate rather than a single best setting.
explanation:
### Why this chart and not another

The appendix this figure sits in is about picking hyperparameters, and it opens by admitting the paper has no single number that tracks what it cares about. [[dictionary-learning]] here has two knobs: how wide the dictionary is, and how hard the [[l1-sparsity-penalty]] pushes. Two of the proxies the paper does trust pull against each other. The [[l0-norm]] — the average count of features with a nonzero activation on a token — should be small, or the code is not really sparse. The share of the MLP's loss contribution the features reproduce, the paper's [[loss-recovered-by-features]] measure, should be large, or the features are not explaining the model.

A table of runs would invite sorting by one column, which quietly picks a winner. A bar chart of the best score per penalty setting would throw away the sparsity a run paid for it. An average across runs would erase the knobs entirely, which is the only thing the appendix is trying to talk about. Putting one [[dictionary-learning-run]] at its own coordinates is what makes the exchange rate visible: you can see what a point of explained behaviour costs in active features, and see that the cost is not constant.

### How to read it, step by step

The horizontal axis is average $L^0$, linear, running from about 4 to 20 features active per token. Left is sparser. It is the realised sparsity, not the requested one, which is why it is the axis rather than the penalty weight. The vertical axis is the explained fraction, from about 0.67 to 0.945: run the transformer, pass its MLP activations through the [[sparse-autoencoder]], splice the reconstruction back in, and measure how much the loss rises; divide that rise by the rise from deleting the MLP entirely ([[zero-ablation-baseline]]) and subtract from one. The label says "Percent" but the ticks are fractions.

One dot is one finished autoencoder. Colour is the [[l1-coefficient]] $\lambda$ — four values, 0.004 through 0.01. Each coloured line joins six dictionary sizes ([[expansion-factor]] from 1x up to 256x the MLP's 512 neurons) trained at that one $\lambda$; the line is bookkeeping, not a fit.

Look first at the horizontal gaps between colours: $\lambda$ largely fixes which vertical band a run lands in. Then look along one colour: the climb is nearly vertical. Width buys explanation almost for free in sparsity terms, while loosening the penalty buys it by letting more features fire.

### What a bad result would look like

If the four colours collapsed onto one common curve, the plot would say that $\lambda$ acts only through $L^0$ and that width buys nothing a weaker penalty would not buy more cheaply — a single frontier, pick any point. They do not collapse. Around $L^0 \approx 8$ the green ($\lambda=0.008$) band is near 0.905 while the red ($\lambda=0.006$) band starts near 0.745, so at equal sparsity a wide dictionary under a strong penalty beats a narrow one under a weak penalty. If instead the lines sloped rightwards as width grew, widening would cost sparsity and the cheap-climb reading would fail. And if every run landed above 0.95, the measure would be telling you nothing, which is close to the paper's own worry ([[reconstructed-nll-overestimate-caveat]]): zero-ablating the MLP may be an unusually weak baseline, so these heights are called an overestimate.

### Where it comes back

Nowhere else in this paper — the shape appears once. What returns is the run family. The [[feature-density-histogram]] appendix walks the same six sizes grouped by the same coefficients, and the [[feature-splitting]] section takes three of these dictionaries and shows what widening does to individual features rather than to the aggregate. Read together, this chart is the ledger and those are the itemisation. The paper picks no optimum from it: it says only that it targets $L^0$ below 10 or 20, without a principled reason ([[l0-nll-tradeoff]]).
